2023_033_june_2023_accountability_report.paragraph: Troy School District's June 2023 accountability report, presented to the Board of Education on June 6, 2023, reports progress under the Project 2026 Blueprint on the four World Class for All strategic pillars: Green (Early Childhood to Career), Red (Equity and Well-Being), Blue (Deep Learning) and Gold (Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families). Each pillar is reported through objectives, key results, celebrations, challenges and recommendations spanning November 2022 through June 2023. Among the most consequential items, the Portrait of a Graduate has completed Phases 1-3 following a January Board workshop and is awaiting Board adoption, and the district reports 2023-24 early childhood capacity of GSRP 80 max, PreK 90/100 and ECP 96 max.
2023_033_june_2023_accountability_report.page:
**Document**
June 2023 Accountability Report (PDF handout of the Project 2026 Blueprint presentation), Troy School District Board of Education meeting of June 6, 2023.

**Framing: Clarifying Our Foundation**
The foundation is presented as four elements: Mission (Why do we exist? / fundamental purpose / clarifies priorities and sharpens focus); Vision (What must our school become to accomplish our purpose? / compelling future / gives directions); Values (How must we behave to achieve our vision? / collective commitments / guides behaviors); and Goals (How will we mark our progress? / targets and timelines / establish priorities).

**(Re)Design Process: See, Engage, Act**
SEE draws on system-level data across demographic, process, academic and perception categories. ENGAGE means planning with key stakeholders including students, the BOE and staff. ACT means redesigning with Strategic Planning Teams, reviewing with the BOE, and finalizing strategic planning in June.

**Green Pillar - Early Childhood to Career**
Objectives: continue investing in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for universal preschool access for all three- and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, including career and technical education, computer science access, connections for underrepresented students to in-demand careers, and work-based learning, credentials and college credit. Key results (updated June 2023) cover early and frequent 2023-24 recruitment, preschool-to-kindergarten transition, monitoring of preschool impact on achievement data and of access across the district, and Portrait of a Graduate adoption in progress. Celebrations include 2023-24 early childhood enrollment (full-day and half-day AM tuition full with additional sections opening in 23-24; GSRP 80 max with additional requested, income threshold expansion and a shift to Morse, Troy Union, Hill and Wass; Strong Beginnings free three-year-old program; PreK 90/100 with an added section; ECP 96 max), a Kindergarten Transition Committee, the January BoE workshop with Phases 1-3 complete, K-8 career readiness with Media Specialists and Maker Space growth, Early Middle College with LTU, a Business Round Table, and digital portfolio prep tied to Xello.

**Red Pillar - Equity and Well-Being**
Objectives: fund additional investments supporting the whole child, elevate Alignment, Access and Agency district wide, and assess needs to meet world-class learning environment demands. January-June 2023 results: re-energizing the Red Pillar, establishing the district JEDI Council and equity webpage, a Tier One elementary SEL curriculum pilot, CSTAG self-harm trainings for psychologists and social workers, a Middle School Advisory Study Team, a completed student code of conduct review, NEP Day of Learning/ILT, and the 2022-23 Equity Analysis Survey and listening tours. Hanover recommendations call for deeper equity professional learning, heavy focus on bullying, and prioritizing diversity resources and gender identities and expression.

**Blue Pillar - Deep Learning**
Objectives cover MTSS systems of support and student voice, technology access and training, global best practices (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships), and upgraded facilities. Key results: Math Recovery training for elementary resource and teacher consultants, Celebrations of Learning at middle schools, authentic assessments including interviews and digital portfolios, adoption of elementary and middle school math curriculum, and media curriculum work with Dr. Edward Clapp.

**Gold Pillar - Building Capacity**
Objectives address educator preparation, pipelines for underrepresented educators, job-embedded professional learning, and co-designed learning for the OneTroy community. Key results include an Academics website, an Eastern Michigan University scholarship program for existing employees, Student Support Aide orientation and mentoring, a sub-cabinet team covering budget, staffing and professional learning, and partnerships with OU (secondary), EMU (special education) and WSU (social work). A years-of-service display lists 15+, 20+ and 25+ with the figures 127, 114 and 78.
2023_033_june_2023_accountability_report.verbose:
Title and setting: "June 2023 Accountability Report," a PDF of the Project 2026 Blueprint presentation prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of June 6, 2023. The cover identifies the district as Troy School District and the initiative as the Project 2026 Blueprint.

Clarifying Our Foundation. The opening section lays out the foundational architecture of the plan in four parts. Mission answers "Why? Why do we exist?" and is described as the FUNDAMENTAL PURPOSE that clarifies priorities and sharpens focus. Vision answers "WHAT? What must our school become to accomplish our purpose?" and is described as the COMPELLING FUTURE that gives directions. Values answer "HOW? How must we behave to achieve our vision?" and are described as COLLECTIVE COMMITMENTS that guide behaviors. Goals answer "HOW WILL WE MARK OUR PROGRESS?" and are described as TARGETS AND TIMELINES that establish priorities.

(Re)Design Process: See, Engage, Act. The SEE phase uses system-level data spanning demographic, process, academic and perception data. The ENGAGE phase involves planning with key stakeholders, specifically students, the BOE and staff. The ACT phase involves redesigning WITH Strategic Planning Teams, reviewing with the BOE, and a June milestone to finalize strategic planning.

Accountability Plan. The report states that the World Class for All pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results. Four pillars are reported: Green (Early Childhood to Career), Red (Equity and Well-Being), Blue (Deep Learning) and Gold (Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families).

Green Pillar objectives. Continue to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for access to universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds. Expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, with a plan aimed at providing more students access to high-quality career and technical education programs that expand access to computer science; connect underrepresented students to careers in demand in high-growth industry sectors; and build partnerships with institutions of higher education, employers and other stakeholders that allow students to engage in quality work-based learning opportunities, earn a credential, and/or earn college credit.

Green Pillar key results, updated June 2023. Early childhood recruitment for 2023-24 described as early and frequent. Focus on meaningful transition from preschool to kindergarten. Monitoring of the impact of preschool on achievement data and monitoring of access across the district. Portrait of a Graduate adoption in progress. A slide titled "TSD Preschool Access Overtime" accompanies this section.

Green Pillar celebrations, November 2022 through June 2023. Under 2023-24 Early Childhood Enrollment: Tuition full-day and half-day AM programs are full, with additional sections opening in 23-24; GSRP is listed at 80 max with additional capacity requested, an income threshold expansion, and a shift to Morse, Troy Union, Hill and Wass to increase access; Strong Beginnings is described as a free three-year-old program; PreK is listed as 90/100 with an additional section added; ECP is listed at 96 max. A Kindergarten Transition Committee is noted along with a visual timeline. Under Portrait of Graduate: a January BoE Workshop was held, Phases 1-3 are complete, and BoE adoption is coming soon. Career readiness engagement opportunities for K-8 are partnered with Media Specialists and Maker Space growth. The district continues to prioritize post-secondary learning partnerships throughout K-12, including Early Middle College with LTU and a Business Round Table. Preparation for digital portfolios involves K-5 media, middle school innovation coaches and 6-8 English teachers, tied to Xello and future-ready exit discussions with students.

Green Pillar challenges, November 2022 through June 2023. Cohesion of programming during the 2023-24 shift; identifying barriers to preschool access; alignment of Media/Maker with Career Readiness, specifically training (time) and consistency (buy-in); shifting the mindset around the stigma of career readiness to prioritize relevance to learning in classrooms; supporting high school building leaders in embedding career readiness initiatives; and keeping Portrait of a Graduate on timeline while leveraging its connection to the current strategic plan.

Green Pillar June 2023 recommendations. Continue ongoing preschool recruitment and hold a Preschool Summer Institute 2023. Continue prioritizing messaging career readiness as a tool for students aligned with academic planning and college readiness with administrators, teachers and counselors. Continue focusing on business partnerships to enhance work-based learning for all high school students. Expand TSD Learning Portfolios to all students in Grades 3-9. Prioritize digital citizenship for K-8. Continue to expand embedded career readiness initiatives K-8 via media and elective classes. Jump start TSD's computer science K-12 curriculum collaboration with the Oakland Schools Computer Science team. Secure Portrait of Graduate board adoption and key stakeholder support.

Red Pillar objectives. Ensuring a focus on equity and well-being; funding additional investments to support the needs of the whole child; an elevated focus on Alignment, Access and Agency district wide; and assessing needs and taking action to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.

Red Pillar celebrations and key results, January through June 2023. Re-establishing and re-energizing the district Red Pillar. Establishing a district level equity team, the JEDI Council, and an equity webpage. A Tier One SEL curriculum pilot at the elementary level. CSTAG self-harm trainings for school psychologists and social workers. A Middle School Advisory Study Team established and progressing. A completed student code of conduct review. Emphasis on adult learning in well-being and equity through the NEP Day of Learning and ILT. An Equity Analysis Survey for 2022-23 along with listening tours.

Red Pillar looking ahead to 2023-2024. Diversify and expand the Red Pillar team around Alignment, Access and Agency. Expand the SEL curriculum pilot. Transform adult SEL. Develop professional learning and community learning series models with an equity focus. Investigate wraparound services such as afterschool programs specific to SEL and equity. Partner with the Director of Security to review safety protocols. Conduct focused group work dedicated to establishing consistent MTSS structures. Run a book study and workshop series including Culturally Responsive Teaching and Street Data.

Red Pillar challenges and recommendations. Elevated concerns and needs include encouraging and implementing aligned structures, equity teamwork across buildings, and SEL and MTSS curriculum. Hanover recommendations are to dive deeper into professional learning for staff in the areas of equity, focus heavily on issues of bullying, and prioritize diversity including resources district wide and gender identities and expression. The report also calls for continued social work, psychologist and counseling support in all buildings and work toward more cohesive relationships and levels of support across all buildings.

Blue Pillar objectives. Create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice through MTSS, with access to deep learning described as imperative for all children. Improve technology access for students and families while providing quality training to leverage technology to deepen learning. Continue to pursue global best practices in all content areas, citing NPDL, The 6 C's and learning partnerships. Assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.

Blue Pillar key results. Elementary resource and teacher consultants trained in Math Recovery Training. Celebrations of Learning at middle schools. Continued pursuit of authentic assessments such as interviews and digital portfolios. Adoption of elementary and middle school math curriculum rooted in pedagogy. Elementary and middle school media teams continuing to develop curriculum using inquiry and maker-centered practices, with secondary engaged in this learning, in partnership with Dr. Edward Clapp. Elementary MTSS work continues to monitor benchmark data and develop capacity in math; secondary MTSS work continues to define roles on the MTSS team and consider data to be utilized.

Blue Pillar next year's work. Learning with outside experts on interdepartmental systems of support; a renewed commitment to instructional practices that foster deep learning across the curriculum; exploring quality interim assessment tools for core areas; continuing to grow digital portfolios for students to document learning over time; and continued elementary and middle school media team curriculum development using inquiry and maker-centered practices.

Gold Pillar objectives. Improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators and supporting current educators; continuing to provide job-embedded professional learning experiences for all staff; and providing professional learning opportunities for staff, community and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community.

Gold Pillar key results. Development of an Academics website for parent and community communication. A scholarship program currently being developed with Eastern Michigan University for existing employees. A Student Support Aide orientation, mentoring and training process. A sub-cabinet team for creating coherence covering budget, staffing and professional learning. Expanded partnerships with OU (secondary), EMU (special education) and WSU (social work). A years-of-service display lists the categories 15+, 20+ and 25+ alongside the figures 127, 114 and 78. Job-embedded tech learning for all core secondary staff. A hosted parent learning series with Celebrate Hope and Dr. Tony Wagner. High school 9th and 10th grade ELA teams continuing to develop curriculum. Learning with Dr. Jonathan Bostic and Illustrative Mathematics for middle school math teachers. Learning with Dr. Ted Coe for high school mathematics. Learning with Dr. Israel Tatou on design of physics curriculum. Use of late-start days to prioritize conversations with collaborative teacher teams around student learning.

Gold Pillar next year's work. Continued partnership with Celebrate Hope; job-embedded tech learning; implementation of professional learning in mathematics to support the new curriculum; enhanced learning opportunities for support staff; culturally and linguistically responsive teaching practices embedded into all job-embedded learning; continued investigation into attracting experienced staff from outside the district; retention strategies; and a "Grow Your Own" strategy for recruitment, both county and Troy-specific.

Closing. The report ends with a "What's Next?" quotation: "The world's best school systems ensure that all stakeholders understand the purpose, priorities, and goals of the system. Leaders clarify a few very specific non-negotiables that must be honored throughout the system and at the same time they encourage autonomy and creativity at all levels to foster ownership and innovation."

2023_035_sarah_young_resume.paragraph: Resume of Sarah Young, EdS, BCBA, included in the Troy School District Board of Education packet for the meeting of May 16, 2023. Young has served as Troy School District's Supervisor of Special Education since July 2018, following roles as the district's Behavior Support Coordinator from July 2015 to August 2018 and as a special education teacher in the ASD program at Morse Elementary School from August 2010 to July 2015. Her credentials include an Education Specialist degree from Wayne State University in Central Office Administration and Special Education Leadership and Board Certified Behavior Analyst certification.

**Candidate**
Sarah Young, EdS, BCBA. Contact listed as syoung@troy.k12.mi.us and 248-563-5343. Submitted in the Troy School District Board of Education packet dated May 16, 2023.

**Summary**
Self-described as a compassionate, positive-minded leader with commitment, knowledge and desire to contribute to special education, district and county leadership, and applied behavior analysis, building relationships with staff, students and families through proactive support, visibility and responsiveness.

**Skills**
Behavior analysis; complex problem solving and meeting facilitation; program development and support structures; professional development planning and facilitation; relationship building; recruiting and hiring; special education legal adherence; staff leadership and evaluation.

**Experience**

| Role | Organization | Dates |
| --- | --- | --- |

2023_036_middle_school_mathematics_revie.page:
**Document**
Middle School Mathematics Materials Adoption, May 2023, submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Kate Rainey to the Troy School District Board of Education, meeting date May 16, 2023.

**Rationale**
Troy School District reviews curricular materials every nine years. The district's philosophy has shifted from simply seeking new materials toward a comprehensive look at programming, including instructional practices, intervention, assessment and current data, so that curricular, structural and staffing needs can be aligned. The last middle school math adoption was conducted in 2012. Since then the district reports better understanding of the Michigan Math State Standards, better-aligned middle school math resources, and continued guidance from the National Council for Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM). Teachers have been supplementing the current resource with problem-based tasks, number sense routines and additional materials; a resource addressing both deep conceptual learning and mathematical fluency is desired.

**Process and selection**
A Middle School Math Pilot Team was assembled with representation from all grade levels and buildings. Members engaged with Catalyzing Change (NCTM) and Building Thinking Classrooms (Liljedhal, 2021), and the district continued its partnership with professor Jonathan Bostic of Bowling Green State University. The team established a vision aligned to the strategic plan, then built a rubric with criteria drawn from each pillar. Eight resources were previewed: Mid-School Math; College-Preparatory Mathematics (CPM); Agile Mind; Big Ideas; Desmos; Amplify; Connected Mathematics Project (CMP); and Illustrative Mathematics (IM). The review matrix narrowed the field to CMP and IM.

**Pilot team roster**
Boulan: Jordan Baines (Math 6 and Math 6/7), Michelle Tasich (Math 6 and Math 6/7), Kristy D'Ambrosi (Math 8), A.J. Scovoronski (Math Specialist). Baker: Sree Bollavaram (Math 8), Jamie VanTiem (Math 7), Andrew LaTorre (Math Specialist). Smith: Taryn Huang (Math 6), Cherie Maher (Math 7, Math 7/8), Brad Pyke (Math 8), Melissa Rehbine (Math Specialist). Larson: Wendy Wilcox (Math 6, Math 6/7), Shelley McHugh (Math 7), Hadeel Yousif (Math 8), Lyndsey Becker (Math 8), Mark Hayes (Math Specialist).

**Pilot process and professional learning**
Each pilot teacher committed to teaching at least two units from both CMP and IM, with some teaching more. CMP was used in semester one and IM in semester two. Professional learning included 1.5 days during the school day for all piloting teachers prior to the start of each pilot; 4 job-embedded opportunities per pilot teacher; job-embedded technology and pilot curriculum learning for all middle school math teachers; 2 days of district PD on best practice and pedagogy with Dr. Bostic and MSU facilitators; PLC meetings supported with building subs; co-planning, co-teaching and coaching by math specialists; and paid after-hours work. Data collected included student and teacher surveys, work samples, videos and assessments.

**Findings**
CMP strengths: multiple ways for students to solve problems, deepened learning through talk and collaboration, and sufficient support for some teachers. CMP challenges: concerns about being invitational and relevant, materials not manageable to use, and supporting all learners. The summary concludes the CMP learning platform is not developed enough to support daily use. IM strengths: invites all students into the mathematics, multiple solution paths, learning deepened through talk and collaboration, manageable teacher materials with enough guidance, sufficient support for fidelity, and teacher confidence to implement. IM challenges: more guidance on fostering an engaging learning environment and more professional learning on supporting all learners.

**Recommendation and projected costs (Grades 6-8 Mathematics)**

| Item | Projected cost |
| --- | --- |
| Illustrative Mathematics curriculum provided by Imagine Learning Classroom (online platform, student workbooks, teacher editions) | $110,000 per year |
| Formal learning partnership with Illustrative Mathematics staff developers: 3 days per grade level x 3 grade levels = 9 professional learning days @ $3,000 per day | $27,000 per year |
| Other materials such as manipulatives and consumables: 25 teachers x 100/teacher | $2,500 per year |
| Total | $139,500 per year |

**Implementation**
The pilot team worked over three sessions to create an implementation plan for all staff, including job-embedded learning, planning sessions and optional summer learning.
2023_036_middle_school_mathematics_revie.verbose:
Document and authorship. "Middle School Mathematics Materials Adoption," dated May 2023, submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Kate Rainey for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of May 16, 2023.

Rationale. The report states that in the Troy School District curricular materials are regularly reviewed every nine years. Since the last curricular adoption the district has updated its philosophy regarding curricular review, having learned through work in other areas that taking a comprehensive look at programming is an essential part of the review process. It is not enough to simply seek new materials; the district also needs to take stock of current programming, including understanding instructional practices, intervention, assessment, and current data. By examining opportunities in their entirety, the district can align curricular, structural, and staffing needs.

The last middle school math adoption was conducted in 2012. Since that time, the report says, much has taken place in the field of mathematics and in Troy classrooms: the district now better understands the Michigan Math State Standards, there are better aligned resources for middle school math available, and the national math organization, the National Council for Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM), has continued to develop learning and guidance around best practice in mathematics teaching and learning. In recent years Troy teachers have been supplementing the current resource with problem-based tasks, number sense routines, and additional materials to address missed opportunities. A new resource that fully addresses deep conceptual learning as well as mathematical fluency is desired.

Process and selection. To begin the review, the district assembled the Middle School Math Pilot Team, an interdepartmental group with representation from all grade levels and buildings across the system, providing a variety of perspectives to ensure broad development of shared understanding. Throughout the review process, members engaged in learning from Catalyzing Change (NCTM) and Building Thinking Classrooms (Liljedhal, 2021). The district also continued its partnership with professor Jonathan Bostic from Bowling Green State University.

Pilot team roster by building and assignment. From Boulan: Jordan Baines, Teacher, Math 6 and Math 6/7; Michelle Tasich, Teacher, Math 6 and Math 6/7; Kristy D'Ambrosi, Teacher, Math 8; A.J. Scovoronski, Math Specialist. From Baker: Sree Bollavaram, Math 8; Jamie VanTiem, Math 7; Andrew LaTorre, Math Specialist. From Smith: Taryn Huang, Math 6; Cherie Maher, Math 7 and Math 7/8; Brad Pyke, Math 8; Melissa Rehbine, Math Specialist. From Larson: Wendy Wilcox, Math 6 and Math 6/7; Shelley McHugh, Math 7; Hadeel Yousif, Math 8; Lyndsey Becker, Math 8; Mark Hayes, Math Specialist.

The team first established a vision for teaching and learning in mathematics that aligns to the district strategic plan, then created a rubric to vet potential resources, with each pillar represented by criteria to review. The goal was to ensure that resources chosen for pilot match the strategic plan and the vision for teaching and learning in mathematics. The team previewed eight different resources: Mid-School Math; College-Preparatory Mathematics (CPM); Agile Mind; Big Ideas; Desmos; Amplify; Connected Mathematics Project (CMP); and Illustrative Mathematics (IM). The review matrix was used to narrow the field down to two resources, Connected Mathematics Project and Illustrative Mathematics.

Pilot process. Each teacher from the pilot team committed to teaching at least two units from both CMP and IM, and some taught more than two. Connected Mathematics Project was utilized in semester one and Illustrative Math in semester two. Pilot teachers were provided support through professional development throughout the process.

Professional learning during the pilot. 1.5 days of professional learning was provided during the school day to all piloting teachers prior to the start of each pilot. 4 job-embedded professional learning opportunities were offered to every pilot teacher during the piloting experience. All middle school math teachers engaged in job-embedded professional learning around technology and the pilot curriculum. During district PD, all teachers engaged in 2 days of learning on best practice and pedagogy with Dr. Bostic and MSU facilitators. Pilot teachers met as PLCs, supported with building subs. Math specialists co-planned, co-taught, and coached teachers throughout the pilot. Pilot teachers were paid to work after hours.

Data collected. Student and teacher surveys, work samples, videos, and assessments. After each pilot, teachers filled out a survey indicating the strengths and weaknesses of each program and revisited the review matrix.

Resource reflections, Connected Mathematics Project (CMP). Strengths: the curriculum provides multiple ways for students to solve problems; the curriculum allows students to deepen their learning through talk and collaboration; some teachers believed support provided has been sufficient to implement with fidelity. Challenges: some concerns about the curriculum being invitational and relevant to students; many concerns about providing enough guidance, with materials not manageable to use; some concerns about supporting the needs of all learners. Summary: while the pilot team appreciated many aspects of the learning opportunities with CMP, the learning platform is not developed enough to support the daily use of this curriculum, and teachers shared concerns that this program would be more difficult to implement.

Resource reflections, Illustrative Mathematics (IM). Strengths: the curriculum invites all students into the mathematics; the curriculum provides multiple ways for students to solve problems; the curriculum allows students to deepen their learning through talk and collaboration; teacher materials provide enough guidance and are manageable to use; teacher support has been sufficient to implement with fidelity; teachers feel confident to implement this curriculum. Challenges: more guidance desired about fostering an engaging learning environment; more professional learning desired on supporting the needs of all learners. Summary: Illustrative Mathematics provides support for teachers daily, and teachers shared that the Imagine Learning Classroom learning platform support is extremely responsive to their needs when they have questions and provides all of the resources needed for daily teaching.

Materials recommendation. Illustrative Mathematics is recommended to move forward, along with the purchase of the Imagine Learning Classroom online platform. Estimated costs for curricular resources and implementation support are given for Grades 6-8 Mathematics. The Illustrative Mathematics curriculum provided by Imagine Learning Classroom, which includes the online platform as well as student workbooks and teacher editions, is listed at $110,000 per year. A formal learning partnership with Illustrative Mathematics staff developers, described as 3 days per grade level times 3 grade levels for 9 professional learning days at $3,000 per day, is listed at $27,000 per year. Other materials to support the curriculum, such as manipulatives and consumables, calculated as 25 teachers times 100 per teacher, are listed at $2,500 per year. The total is stated as $139,500 per year.

Implementation plan. The pilot team worked over the course of three sessions to create an implementation plan for all staff, including job-embedded learning, planning sessions, and optional summer learning.
